cards.q: What is the difference between an aldehyde and a ketone?
cards.a: Both contain the carbonyl group, \(\mathrm{C=O}\). In an aldehyde it is at the end of the chain (\(\mathrm{-CHO}\)); in a ketone it is between two carbon atoms (\(\mathrm{R-CO-R'}\)).
cards.why: So an aldehyde’s carbonyl carbon carries at least one H; a ketone’s carries none.

cards.q: Name this compound and say whether it is an aldehyde or a ketone.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a three-carbon chain ending in a C=O group with an H on the carbonyl carbon.

cards.a: Propanal, an aldehyde.
cards.why: The suffix -al means an aldehyde; the carbonyl carbon is carbon 1, so no number is needed.

cards.q: Give the name of this compound and the homologous series it belongs to.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a four-carbon chain with a C=O group on the second carbon.

cards.a: Butanone, a ketone.
cards.why: In butanone the C=O can only be on carbon 2 (carbon 3 is the same from the other end), so no number is needed.

cards.q: Name this compound.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a four-carbon chain ending in a CHO group, with a methyl branch on the carbon furthest from the CHO.

cards.a: 3-methylbutanal
cards.why: Number from the aldehyde carbon (carbon 1); the methyl group is on carbon 3.

cards.q: Name this ketone.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a five-carbon chain with a C=O group on the middle carbon.

cards.a: Pentan-3-one
cards.why: Its isomer pentan-2-one has the C=O on carbon 2.

cards.q: Is this compound an aldehyde or a ketone?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of cyclohexanone: a six-membered carbon ring with a C=O group on one ring carbon.

cards.a: A ketone (cyclohexanone).
cards.why: The carbonyl carbon is bonded to two other carbon atoms in the ring.

cards.q: Give the structural formula of ethanal and of propanone.
cards.a:
Ethanal: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CHO}\).
Propanone: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3}}\).
cards.why: Write an aldehyde group as \(\mathrm{CHO}\), never \(\mathrm{COH}\), which looks like an alcohol.

cards.q: Propanal and butane have similar relative molecular masses. Explain why propanal has the higher boiling temperature, but a lower one than propan-1-ol.
cards.a: Propanal has permanent dipole–dipole forces but, unlike propan-1-ol, cannot hydrogen bond to itself.
marks: Propanal has a polar \(\mathrm{C=O}\) bond, so there are permanent dipole–dipole forces between its molecules as well as London forces.
Butane is non-polar and has only London forces, so propanal boils higher.
Propanal has no H bonded to O (or N, F), so it cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
Propan-1-ol has an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group and forms hydrogen bonds, which are stronger, so propan-1-ol boils higher still.

cards.q: Explain why propanone mixes completely with water.

figure.alt: Propanone hydrogen bonding to water: a lone pair on the δ− oxygen of the C=O group forms a hydrogen bond, shown dashed, to the δ+ hydrogen of a water molecule.

cards.a: The lone pairs on the carbonyl oxygen form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
marks: The oxygen of the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) group is δ− and has lone pairs.
It forms a hydrogen bond to a δ+ hydrogen atom of a water molecule.
Energy released forming these hydrogen bonds makes up for breaking some hydrogen bonds between water molecules.

cards.q: How does the solubility in water of aldehydes and ketones change as the carbon chain gets longer, and why?
cards.a: It decreases. The longer non-polar hydrocarbon part cannot hydrogen bond with water.
cards.why: Ethanal and propanone mix completely with water; hexan-2-one is only slightly soluble.

cards.q: True or false: aldehydes and ketones form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules.
cards.a: False. They have no H bonded to O, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
cards.why: They can still hydrogen bond to water, by accepting a hydrogen bond with a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [O], for the oxidation of ethanal by acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CHO + [O] \rightarrow CH_{3}COOH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanal is oxidised to ethanoic acid by acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux.

cards.why: Aldehydes are readily oxidised to carboxylic acids; the orange dichromate turns green.

cards.q: What colour change is seen when an aldehyde is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)? What is seen with a ketone?
cards.a:
Aldehyde: orange to green (\(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\)).
Ketone: stays orange.
cards.why: Ketones are not oxidised under these conditions.

cards.q: Explain why ketones are not oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI), whereas aldehydes are.
cards.a: Oxidising a ketone would need a C–C bond to break.
marks: In an aldehyde, the carbonyl carbon carries an H atom, so it can be oxidised to COOH by adding an O.
In a ketone, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms and has no H.
Further oxidation would need a C–C bond to be broken, which mild oxidising agents cannot do.

cards.q: Describe the Tollens’ test for an aldehyde, including the result for an aldehyde and for a ketone.
cards.a: Warm the compound with Tollens’ reagent in a water bath. An aldehyde gives a silver mirror (or black precipitate); a ketone gives no change.
cards.why: Tollens’ reagent is \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}}\) in ammonia solution: silver(I) ions are reduced to silver metal.

cards.q: Write the half-equation for the reduction of the silver complex in Tollens’ reagent.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Ag + 2NH_{3}}\)
cards.why: The aldehyde is the reducing agent: it is oxidised to a carboxylic acid (as its salt in the alkaline solution).

cards.q: Describe the Fehling’s (or Benedict’s) test for an aldehyde, including the result for an aldehyde and for a ketone.
cards.a: Warm the compound with Fehling’s solution. An aldehyde turns the blue solution to a brick-red precipitate; a ketone stays blue.
cards.why: Blue \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced to copper(I) oxide, \(\mathrm{Cu_{2}O}\), which is the red precipitate.

cards.q: Why are the Tollens’ and Fehling’s tests warmed in a hot water bath rather than over a Bunsen flame?
cards.a: Aldehydes and ketones are volatile and flammable, so a naked flame must be kept away.
cards.why: A water bath also heats gently and evenly.

cards.q: You have two unlabelled bottles: propanal and propanone. Describe one chemical test that tells them apart.
cards.a: Warm each with Tollens’ reagent: propanal gives a silver mirror, propanone does not. (Or Fehling’s: propanal gives a brick-red precipitate, propanone stays blue.)
cards.why: Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, so that test cannot tell them apart.

cards.q: True or false: propanone gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent because it contains a C=O group.
cards.a: False. Only aldehydes give the silver mirror; propanone is a ketone and is not oxidised.
cards.why: Tollens’ and Fehling’s tests depend on the compound being oxidised, not on the C=O group itself.

cards.q: What is formed when (a) an aldehyde and (b) a ketone is reduced?
cards.a:
(a) A primary alcohol.
(b) A secondary alcohol.
cards.why: Reduction adds two hydrogen atoms across the C=O bond.

cards.q: Which reducing agent and conditions does AQA specify for reducing aldehydes and ketones to alcohols?
cards.a: Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III), \(\mathrm{NaBH_{4}}\), in aqueous solution (or in ethanol).
cards.why: \(\mathrm{NaBH_{4}}\) supplies hydride ions, \(\mathrm{H^{-}}\), which act as the nucleophile.

cards.q: Which reducing agent does Edexcel specify for reducing aldehydes and ketones, and why must the solvent be dry?
cards.a: Lithium tetrahydridoaluminate, \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) (lithium aluminium hydride), in dry ether.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) reacts violently with water, releasing hydrogen.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [H], for the reduction of propanal.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CHO + 2[H] \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}OH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: propanal is reduced to propan-1-ol by NaBH4 in aqueous solution.

cards.why: Two [H] are added: one H to the carbon and one to the oxygen.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [H], for the reduction of propanone.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3} + 2[H] \rightarrow CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3}}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: propanone is reduced to propan-2-ol by NaBH4 in aqueous solution.

cards.why: The product, propan-2-ol, is a secondary alcohol.

cards.q: What type of reaction is the reduction of a carbonyl compound by NaBH<sub>4</sub>, and what is the nucleophile?
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition. The nucleophile is the hydride ion, \(\mathrm{H^{-}}\).
cards.why: \(\mathrm{H^{-}}\) adds to the δ+ carbon; the oxygen then gains \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from water.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reduction of propanal by NaBH<sub>4</sub>.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition: hydride attacks the carbonyl carbon, then the alkoxide ion takes a proton from water.

answerFigure.alt: Nucleophilic addition of hydride to propanal: the lone pair on H− attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond breaks onto oxygen; the O− of the intermediate takes H+ from water, giving propan-1-ol.

marks: Curly arrow from the lone pair on \(\mathrm{H^{-}}\) to the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
Curly arrow from the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) double bond to the oxygen.
Correct intermediate, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}O^{-}}\), with its negative charge on O.
Curly arrow from a lone pair on \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) to an H of water (or to \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\)), giving propan-1-ol.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reduction of propanone to propan-2-ol by NaBH<sub>4</sub>.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition of H⁻, then protonation of the alkoxide ion by water.

answerFigure.alt: Nucleophilic addition of hydride to propanone: H− attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond breaks onto oxygen; the alkoxide oxygen takes H+ from water, giving propan-2-ol.

marks: Lone pair on \(\mathrm{H^{-}}\) attacks the δ+ carbon of \(\mathrm{C=O}\).
The π bond of \(\mathrm{C=O}\) breaks, the electrons moving onto O.
Intermediate \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{2}CHO^{-}}\).
\(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) lone pair takes \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from water, forming \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{2}CHOH}\).

cards.q: Explain why the carbonyl group is attacked by nucleophiles, whereas the C=C bond of an alkene is attacked by electrophiles.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C=O}\) is polar, with a δ+ carbon; \(\mathrm{C=C}\) is non-polar and electron-rich.
marks: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar.
The carbonyl carbon is δ+ and is attacked by nucleophiles (electron-pair donors).
The C=C bond is non-polar with a region of high electron density in the π bond, which attracts electrophiles instead.

cards.q: True or false: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces but-3-enal, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CHO, to butan-1-ol.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of but-3-enal: a four-carbon chain with a C=C double bond at one end and a CHO group at the other.

cards.a: False. Only the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) is reduced, giving but-3-en-1-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_{2}=CHCH_{2}CH_{2}OH}\).
cards.why: \(\mathrm{H^{-}}\) is a nucleophile: it attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon but not the non-polar \(\mathrm{C=C}\).

cards.q: Write an overall equation for the reaction of ethanal with HCN, and name the product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CHO + HCN \rightarrow CH_{3}CH(OH)CN}\)
2-hydroxypropanenitrile.

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanal is converted to 2-hydroxypropanenitrile by KCN followed by dilute acid; overall, HCN is added across the C=O bond.

cards.why: The carbon chain grows by one carbon: the nitrile carbon counts in the name.

cards.q: Write an overall equation for the reaction of propanone with HCN, and name the product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3} + HCN \rightarrow (CH_{3})_{2}C(OH)CN}\)
2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: propanone is converted to 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile by KCN followed by dilute acid; overall, HCN adds across the C=O bond.

cards.why: The longest chain including the nitrile carbon has three carbons, with OH and CH3 on carbon 2.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethanal with KCN followed by dilute acid.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition: \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) attacks the carbonyl carbon, then the alkoxide ion is protonated.

answerFigure.alt: Nucleophilic addition of cyanide to ethanal: the lone pair on the carbon of CN− attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond breaks onto oxygen; the O− intermediate takes H+ to give 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.

marks: Curly arrow from the lone pair on the carbon of \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) to the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
Curly arrow from the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) bond to the oxygen.
Correct intermediate with \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\).
Curly arrow from a lone pair on \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) (or to the H of HCN or water).

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of butanone with HCN in the presence of KCN.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) adds to the carbonyl carbon; the alkoxide ion then takes \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from HCN, regenerating \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\).

answerFigure.alt: Nucleophilic addition of cyanide to butanone: CN− attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond breaks onto oxygen; the O− intermediate takes the H of an HCN molecule, giving 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile and regenerating CN−.

marks: Lone pair on C of \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; dipole on \(\mathrm{C=O}\) shown.
π bond of \(\mathrm{C=O}\) breaks onto O, giving the alkoxide intermediate.
\(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) lone pair attacks the δ+ H of \(\mathrm{H-CN}\); the H–C bond breaks, re-forming \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\).
Product: 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile, formed as a racemic mixture.

cards.q: In the addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound, why is KCN added?
cards.a: HCN is a weak acid and gives very few \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) ions. KCN supplies plenty of \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\), the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) is regenerated when the intermediate takes \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from HCN, so it acts as a catalyst.

cards.q: What are the hazards of using KCN, and how are they controlled?
cards.a: KCN is highly toxic if swallowed or absorbed; with acid it releases HCN, a very toxic gas. Wear gloves, use a fume cupboard, and add the acid with care.
cards.why: This is why KCN followed by dilute acid is used rather than handling HCN gas directly.

cards.q: Explain why the reaction of ethanal with KCN followed by dilute acid gives a product that is optically inactive.
cards.a: The planar \(\mathrm{C=O}\) is attacked equally from both sides, giving a racemic mixture.
marks: The product, 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, has a chiral centre.
The carbonyl group (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)) is planar.
\(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) can attack from either side (above or below the plane) with equal probability.
Equal amounts of the two enantiomers form: a racemic mixture, which does not rotate plane-polarised light.

cards.q: Which of these give a racemic mixture with HCN/KCN: methanal, propanal, propanone, butanone?
cards.a: Propanal and butanone. Their products have a chiral centre. Methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)) and propanone give products with two identical groups on the carbon, so no chiral centre.
cards.why: Any aldehyde except methanal, and any unsymmetrical ketone, gives a racemate.

cards.q: Name the product of the reaction of butanone with HCN.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of the product: a carbon carrying an OH group, a methyl group, an ethyl group and a C≡N group.

cards.a: 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile
cards.why: The nitrile carbon is carbon 1 of the chain; OH and CH3 are both on carbon 2.

cards.q: What is seen when an aldehyde or ketone is added to 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH, Brady’s reagent)?
cards.a: An orange (or yellow-orange) precipitate forms.
cards.why: This shows a carbonyl group is present but does not tell an aldehyde from a ketone.

cards.q: Describe how the precipitate formed with 2,4-DNPH is used to identify a particular carbonyl compound.
cards.a: Purify the derivative, measure its melting temperature and compare it with data.
marks: Filter off the orange precipitate.
Recrystallise it from a minimum of hot solvent, cool, filter and dry it.
Measure its melting temperature.
Compare with the melting temperatures of the 2,4-DNPH derivatives in a data table: each carbonyl compound gives a different value.

cards.q: An unknown carbonyl compound gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, and no change with Fehling’s solution. The purified derivative melts at 116 °C. Given data for 2,4-DNPH derivatives: propanal 156 °C; propanone 126 °C; butanal 123 °C; butanone 116 °C. Identify the compound.
cards.a: Butanone
steps: No change with Fehling’s: a ketone, not an aldehyde (rules out propanal and butanal).
Melting temperature 116 °C matches the butanone derivative, not propanone (126 °C).
cards.why: Using two tests narrows the list before the melting temperature confirms it.

cards.q: True or false: 2,4-DNPH can be used to tell an aldehyde from a ketone.
cards.a: False. Both give an orange precipitate.
cards.why: Use Tollens’ reagent or Fehling’s solution, which only aldehydes reduce.

cards.q: What is seen when propanone is warmed with iodine in the presence of alkali (sodium hydroxide)?
cards.a: A pale yellow precipitate of triiodomethane, \(\mathrm{CHI_{3}}\), with an antiseptic smell.
cards.why: This is the triiodomethane (iodoform) test.

cards.q: Which structural feature gives a positive result with iodine in alkali?
cards.a: A methyl carbonyl group, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO-}\) (in ethanal and methyl ketones), or a \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)-}\) group (in ethanol and secondary alcohols such as propan-2-ol).
cards.why: Iodine in alkali oxidises \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)-}\) to \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO-}\), which then reacts.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of propanone with iodine and sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3} + 3I_{2} + 4NaOH \rightarrow CHI_{3} + CH_{3}COONa + 3NaI + 3H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: The carboxylate formed has one carbon fewer than the carbonyl compound.

cards.q: Describe a test that distinguishes pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one.
cards.a: Warm each with iodine and sodium hydroxide. Pentan-2-one gives a pale yellow precipitate of triiodomethane; pentan-3-one does not.
cards.why: Only pentan-2-one has a \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO-}\) group. Both are ketones, so Tollens’ and Fehling’s cannot tell them apart.

cards.q: Which of these give a positive triiodomethane test: ethanal, propanal, ethanol, propan-1-ol, butanone?
cards.a: Ethanal, ethanol and butanone.
cards.why: Ethanal and butanone contain \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO-}\); ethanol contains \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)-}\). Propanal and propan-1-ol have neither.

cards.q: Which of these give a positive triiodomethane test? (The figure shows the three compounds.)

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of three compounds side by side: propanone, propanal and propan-2-ol.

cards.a: Propanone and propan-2-ol. Propanal has no \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO-}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)-}\) group.
cards.why: In propanal the carbonyl carbon is at the end of the chain, attached to CH2, not CH3.

cards.q: Starting from propanal, give the reagent for making (a) propanoic acid, (b) propan-1-ol, (c) 2-hydroxybutanenitrile.
cards.a:
(a) Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heat under reflux.
(b) \(\mathrm{NaBH_{4}}\) (aq) (AQA) or \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) in dry ether (Edexcel).
(c) KCN, then dilute acid (or HCN with KCN).
cards.why: Oxidation, reduction and nucleophilic addition: the three reactions of aldehydes in this topic.

cards.q: Why is the reaction of a carbonyl compound with HCN useful in synthesis?
cards.a: It adds a carbon atom to the chain, forming a new C–C bond.
cards.why: The \(\mathrm{-CN}\) group can then be hydrolysed to \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) (or reduced to \(\mathrm{-CH_{2}NH_{2}}\)).
